name: HTTP
summary: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol: stateless requests and responses (a method, a target, header fields, a status code), with one set of semantics carried by three wire versions, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
intro: A client sends a request: a method such as `GET`, `POST`, `PUT` or `DELETE`, a target such as `/orders/4812`, header fields and an optional body. The server answers with a three-digit status code (`2xx` success, `3xx` redirection, `4xx` client error, `5xx` server error), header fields and usually content. HTTP is stateless: each message can be understood on its own, whichever connection it came on, which is what lets proxies reuse connections, caches store responses and load balancers send each request to a different server. Methods carry promises that intermediaries rely on: `GET` and `HEAD` are safe, and `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent, so a request can be retried after a dropped connection. Since 2022 these semantics live in one document, RFC 9110, separate from any wire format; an `http` URL defaults to TCP port 80.

Three versions put those semantics on the wire. HTTP/1.1 (RFC 9112) sends text messages over a persistent TCP connection, one response at a time, so clients open several connections to send requests in parallel. HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) frames messages in binary, interleaves many on one TCP connection and compresses header fields with HPACK, but a single lost TCP packet still stalls every stream. HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) maps the same semantics onto QUIC streams over UDP, with QPACK for fields, so a loss stalls only the request it hit. None of them has replaced the others: clients pick one per connection, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 through TLS negotiation (`h2`, `h3`) and an `Alt-Svc` header that advertises HTTP/3. HTTP inside TLS is HTTPS.
strengths: Spoken by browsers, proxies, CDNs, load balancers and API gateways alike, so a service can be called with nothing more than `curl`
Stateless messages with safe and idempotent methods let intermediaries cache, retry and load-balance without knowing the application
The same semantics on three transports: move from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 without changing a single URL, method or status code
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 multiplex many requests on one connection and compress repetitive headers
limits: Plain `http` is unencrypted and unauthenticated: anyone on the path can read and change requests, so real traffic belongs on HTTPS
HTTP/1.1 has no multiplexing: one slow response blocks the requests behind it on that connection, and pipelining never fixed this because responses must stay in order
HTTP/2 still runs over one TCP connection, so a lost or reordered packet stalls every request in flight
Cleartext HTTP/2 needs prior knowledge that the server supports it (the `h2c` upgrade is deprecated), and HTTP/3 can’t serve `http` URLs directly, only through Alt-Svc

story: Tim Berners-Lee introduced HTTP with the World Wide Web in 1990. The version his 1991 prototype implemented, later called HTTP/0.9, was a single line: the client opened a TCP connection to port 80, sent `GET` and a document address, and the server sent back HTML and closed the connection. Errors were just HTML text; there were no headers or status codes. As the web grew, HTTP gained messages with headers, MIME-style media types and support for intermediaries, documented as HTTP/1.0 in RFC 1945 (May 1996). HTTP/1.1, introduced in 1995 and published in January 1997 as RFC 2068, added chunked transfer, content negotiation, conditional requests, cache controls, range requests and persistent connections by default. It was revised in 1999 (RFC 2616) and again in 2014 (RFCs 7230 to 7235).

In 2009 Google announced SPDY, an experimental protocol that multiplexed streams, prioritised requests and compressed headers; in lab tests pages loaded up to 55% faster. SPDY became the foundation of HTTP/2 (RFC 7540, May 2015). Google’s QUIC work then led to HTTP/3. In June 2022 the IETF reorganised the whole family: RFC 9110 holds the semantics shared by every version, and RFC 9112, RFC 9113 and RFC 9114 define HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 on the wire.

choices.why: Each request can be understood in isolation, so servers keep no per-client state between requests and any proxy, cache or load balancer can sit in the path.

Early HTTP used telnet-style text lines over TCP, which kept every exchange human readable. HTTP/2 moved to binary frames because whitespace-delimited text leads to parsing complexity and can’t multiplex.

choices.choice: Separate semantics from the wire format
choices.why: Splitting RFC 9110 from the version documents lets HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 evolve independently while every method, status code and header field means the same thing in all of them.

timeline.text: Tim Berners-Lee documents the original HTTP, later called HTTP/0.9

RFC 9110 to RFC 9114: shared semantics, plus HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
